title: sustained-throttling-and-recovery-across-gpu-skus
body:
Purpose and motivation:
This is a working note summarizing the 8–12 hour soak runs we ran to probe sustained throttling, soft power/thermal caps, and recovery behaviour across representative cloud SKUs for A100 / H100 / L40S. We want to understand not only steady-state throughput but the *transient* degradation and recovery patterns that affect tail latency and per-token cost when workloads run for long sessions (long-context chat, large-batch decoding, repeated KV-cache churn).

Why this differs from previous benches:
- Prior experiments looked primarily at short-duration microbursts, kernel launch jitter, and driver-version deltas. This exercise intentionally targets multi-hour ramps and step-down/step-up sequences to expose cumulative thermal, clock-throttling, PCIe retraining, and CPU-side backpressure that only appear after sustained utilization.

Quick summary (TL;DR):
- H100 (p5-family equivalent) shows the highest peak throughput but also the most pronounced sustained-clock throttling under AVX-heavy host-side CPU contention unless NVLink is present and KV cache locality is maintained.
- A100 (p4-family) is the most predictable: slower peak but gentler degradation curve and consistent recovery after cool-down windows.
- L40S (l4s-like) delivered consistent single-thread decode performance for small contexts, but sustained multi-session KV write pressure caused PCIe stalls and periodic p99 spikes at ~3–6 hours.
- Driver/CUDA matrix impacted *recovery* behaviour: newer driver stacks (NVIDIA 535+, CUDA 12.x) recovered clocks more aggressively post-cooldown, while older stacks lingered in reduced P-state longer.

Experimental setup (short):
- Instances tested: aws-p4d.24xlarge (A100 40GB), aws-p5.48xlarge (H100 80GB), gcp-l4s-highmem-1 (L40S variant). Mixed cloud zones to represent cross-region variance.
- Software: serving-runtime branch soak/sustained-2024; runtime built with custom kernel-launch batching flags enabled.
- CUDA/driver combos: (a) NVIDIA driver 525 + CUDA 11.8, (b) NVIDIA driver 535 + CUDA 12.1, (c) NVIDIA driver 545 + CUDA 12.2 (where available).
- Load pattern: 3-phase sequence repeated 3x over 12 hours:
  1) Ramp (0 -> 90% GPU util over 20m) with steady decode (seq_len 2048, batch 8) and periodic long-context prefix hits to simulate chat sessions.
  2) Hold (90% util) for 2 hours, tracking power, clocks, PCIe errors, cpu-steal, and tail-latency.
  3) Cooldown (20m of idle) then rapid ramp to 60% util to measure recovery slope.
- Observability: nvml sampling (1s), nsys for 5m windows every hour, eBPF latency traces on host-side RPCs, perf PMU traces for CPU hot functions, and kernel dmesg capture.

Key findings (detailed):
1) Throttling onset and clock trajectories:
- H100 runs consistently reached thermal/power-related clock drops after ~40–50 minutes of sustained 90% utilization on instances without full NVLink (some cloud H100s show NVLink disabled). Clocks fell in ~10–20% steps rather than a continuous slope, leading to discrete throughput drops.
- A100 runs showed a smoother descent; clocks decreased gradually and stabilized at a lower-but-steady operating point.
- L40S showed minimal GPU clock throttling but exhibited host-side stalls (see PCIe/interrupt section).

2) Recovery behaviour (important):
- With driver 535+ the card typically recovered to >95% of pre-throttle clocks within 8–12 minutes of a 20-minute idle window. With older drivers (525+Cuda11.8) cards sometimes took 25–40 minutes to ramp back, with intermediate states that caused p99 flakiness.
- H100 recovery was more sensitive to ambient node temperature and host CPU fan policies (cloud nodes with conservative fan curves prolonged recovery).

3) PCIe/host-side coupling and KV cache churn:
- L40S runs with aggressive KV-cache spill-to-host (our synthetic workload intentionally forced periodic 10% of sessions to repopulate KV) caused a pattern of periodic PCIe completion latency spikes (~ms-level) that pushed decoder tasks to stall; these manifested as p99 latency spikes recurring every ~3–6 hours as DMA queues backed up.
- A100 and H100 with NVLink (where present) absorbed this pressure; without NVLink, both showed degraded steady-state but A100 handled backlog smoothing better.

4) CPU-side saturation and kernel-launch backpressure:
- We observed that host CPU core pinning and governor mode mattered a lot. When CPU cores servicing the runtime were set to ondemand with turbo boost disabled, kernel-launch latencies increased and the GPU ran cooler but with slightly higher per-token latency. Conversely, userspace turbo enabled reduced latency but increased power draw and accelerated thermal throttling on GPUs.
- eBPF traces showed periodic delays in RPC dispatch when kernel schedulers were probed by background system jobs (kubelet updates, cloud agent heartbeat). Those small host-side stalls became amplified by continuous batching and contributed to the observed clock descent.

5) Driver/CUDA quirks observed:
- Driver 545 (when available) improved NVLink error recovery and reduced PCIe link retrain events after long idle periods.
- CUDA 12.x stacks tended to use slightly different default clock governors on some SKUs; this resulted in higher initial clocks, which accelerated entry into thermal throttle during long holds.

Representative numbers (note: synthetic, indicative) – averaged across 3 runs each: 
- Peak tokens/sec (single model, seq=2048, batch=8): H100: 1.0x (baseline 1.0), A100: 0.82x, L40S: 0.46x
- Tokens/sec after 2h sustained (same config): H100: 0.78x (drop ~22%), A100: 0.78x (drop ~22%), L40S: 0.42x (drop ~8% but with intermittent spikes)
- Average p99 latency increase during holds: H100 +38%, A100 +27%, L40S +52% (spike-driven)
- Typical recovery window to within 90% of peak: driver 535+: 8–12m; driver 525: 25–40m

Operational implications for Redwood: 
- SLA design: H100-based SKUs can provide better peak SLAs but we should surface sustained throughput SLOs separately (e.g., 5m rolling vs 2h rolling). On co-tenanted hosts without NVLink, customers may see step-wise degradation that confuses naive autoscalers.
- Routing and fallbacks: For long-running sessions, favor routing to instances with NVLink or to A100 SKU where predictable sustained behaviour matters more than peak. Consider automatic downgrade-to-A100 variant after a continuous 1h hold with p99 deviation >X.
- Cost optimization: cheaper L40S variants are fine for short interactions but require monitoring for PCIe stalls in KV-heavy apps — adding a small KV locality cache on-host (bigger RAM-backed KV) can mitigate.

Immediate next actions / experiments to run:
- Repeat the same soak with ambient-node GPU fan policies varied (where exposed) to confirm recovery sensitivity.
- Isolate NVLink vs PCIe by running identical NVLink-enabled and NVLink-disabled H100 instances and collect link-state logs on retrain events.
- Try a hybrid workload with more frequent small KV hits (typical chat bot) vs fewer large context spills to quantify the PCIe thresholds that trigger spikes.
- Add a test with hyperthreading disabled + realtime kernel tweaks to estimate how much host jitter contributes to GPU throttling.

Open questions / notes to resolve:
- Some cloud images report different powercap defaults; need a canonical mapping: which cloud images set powercap by default and which allow us to change it? (CC: infra team).
- Are there specific EC2 AMIs or GCP images that expose better NVLink configs? We saw variance between zones.
- Should we create a dedicated 'sustained' SKU tag in the console that flags instances tuned/validated for long holds?

References and raw artifacts:
- Raw nvml csvs: link in PR (#812)
- nsys capture samples (hourly): gdrive folder -> /engineering/serving-runtime/soak/nsys-captures/
- Short run checklist used: (attached to PR)

Notes to reviewers:
This doc is intentionally a high-level synthesis for product and infra owners. Team-eng-serving-runtime, please add concrete thresholds for automatic routing policies (e.g., p99 delta > 30% for > 30 minutes -> trigger fallback) and decide if we want an infra ticket to standardize driver stacks across regions.

-- Sofia
(Draft, notes to self and team)
